title: Machine perfusion, 2020–2024
text: This page shows how often each UNOS region used ex vivo machine perfusion (EVMP) for heart transplants from donors after brain death (DBD), from Madan et al. (2025). How to read the maps in general is on Reading the maps.

title: Machine perfusion, 2020–2024
text:
The study in brief
A donor heart is usually carried to the recipient’s hospital on ice, in what is called static cold storage. The longer the heart is without blood flow (the ischemic time), the greater the risk of injury, and hearts from DBD donors are increasingly from older donors and travel longer distances. Ex vivo machine perfusion instead keeps fluid flowing through the heart from a machine outside the body (“ex vivo”) during transport, which could reduce that risk.
The study used the UNOS registry to find the 12,363 adult DBD heart transplants done in the United States from January 2020 to June 2024 that met its criteria: 11,802 with static cold storage and 561 with EVMP. EVMP use rose from 1.4% in the first half of 2020 to 10.7% in the first half of 2024, with large differences between regions and with a few high-volume centers doing most of it. Survival at six months and one year was similar with EVMP and with cold storage, although the EVMP hearts came from older donors, travelled farther and had longer ischemic times (Madan et al. 2025). The map shows the regional part of that finding.

title: Machine perfusion, 2020–2024
text:
What the map shows
Each region is shaded by its own rate of EVMP use: the region’s DBD heart transplants that used EVMP divided by all the region’s DBD heart transplants. Nationally, 561 of 12,363 (4.5%) did.
This is a different kind of percentage from the HCV and DCD maps (see Two kinds of percentage). The rates do not add up to 100%, and a region’s colour does not depend on how many transplants it does. It answers the question when this region did a DBD heart transplant, how often did it use machine perfusion?

title: Machine perfusion, 2020–2024
text:
Reading this map
The darkest region is Region 1, New England: 79 of its 577 DBD heart transplants used EVMP (14%), about three times the national rate. It is small on the main map; the enlarged corridor in the tmap version shows it more clearly.
Next comes Region 11, from Virginia to Tennessee and the Carolinas, at 8% (129 of 1,687). Regions 9 (6%), 6 (5%) and 7 (5%) are also above the national 4.5%. Regions 3 and 10 are close to it (4% each).
The lightest regions are Region 8 in the central Plains (10 of 849, 1%) and Region 2, from Pennsylvania to Washington, DC (19 of 1,247, 2%). Region 4, Texas and Oklahoma, was at 2% and Region 5, from California to New Mexico, at 3%.
The map shows that use of EVMP was not simply a matter of size. Region 5 did more DBD heart transplants than any other region (1,993) but had one of the lower rates, while Region 1 did among the fewest (577) and had the highest.

section: Rate and share tell different stories here
text:
Rate and share tell different stories here
If the map showed each region’s share of the country’s 561 EVMP transplants instead, the picture would change. Region 11 did 129 of them (23%), the most of any region, and would be the darkest; Region 1, with 79 (14%), would come second. Region 5, with 61, would look middling (11%) rather than light.
The published map shows the rate, which answers how often each region chose machine perfusion rather than where most perfused hearts ended up. The table gives the counts, so either can be read from it.

title: Machine perfusion, 2020–2024
text:
Points to keep in mind

A few centers drove most of the use. The paper found that a few high-volume centers did most EVMP transplants (Madan et al. 2025). A region’s rate may therefore reflect one or two centers rather than practice across the region.
A time of rapid change. EVMP use rose from about 1% to about 11% over the study period. The map adds together all four and a half years, so it shows cumulative use, not current practice.
DBD transplants only. The study, and so the map, covered heart transplants from donors after brain death. Transplants from donors after circulatory death are not included.
The rates rest on larger numbers than the other maps. Every region did at least 399 DBD heart transplants, so the rates are steadier than the HCV and DCD shares. The smallest EVMP count was Region 8’s 10.
Whole regions, not states. The map says nothing about where within a region EVMP was used.
The dots are today’s centers. The study ended in June 2024. The dots come from HRSA’s list on the day the map was drawn, and they do not show which centers used EVMP.

title: 4. Machine perfusion (2025)
text: This script draws the regional maps for the study of ex vivo machine perfusion in heart transplantation from donation after brain death (DBD) donors, January 2020 to June 2024, which reported substantial regional variation in its use (Madan et al. 2025).

title: 4. Machine perfusion (2025)
text:
Regional summary
The original map read these counts from a spreadsheet, DBD EVMP UNOS regions_corrected.xlsx; here they are written out in the script with tribble(). The totals are the paper’s: 561 DBD heart transplants with ex vivo machine perfusion out of 12,363. Unlike the HCV and DCD maps, this percentage is each region’s own rate: the share of its DBD transplants that used machine perfusion.
Only the counts are typed in; the percentages are computed from them, so how each is defined can be read in the code. The join to the map stops if any of the eleven regions is missing.


Click to show/hide R Code
# DBD heart transplants by UNOS region, January 2020 to June 2024: all of
# them, and those using ex vivo machine perfusion (EVMP). The totals (12,363
# and 561) are the paper's. The percentage is the share of each region's own
# DBD transplants that used EVMP, as in the regional spreadsheet the original
# map read.
evmp_summary <- tibble::tribble(
  ~region,     ~n_dbd, ~n_evmp,
  "Region 1",     577,      79,
  "Region 2",    1247,      19,
  "Region 3",    1523,      66,
  "Region 4",    1109,      27,
  "Region 5",    1993,      61,
  "Region 6",     399,      21,
  "Region 7",    1069,      53,
  "Region 8",     849,      10,
  "Region 9",     958,      56,
  "Region 10",    952,      40,
  "Region 11",   1687,     129
) |>
  mutate(pct_evmp = 100 * n_evmp / n_dbd)

evmp_measures <- c(
  pct_evmp = "DBD HTs in the region\nusing EVMP (%)"
)

evmp_states <- join_region_values(region_states, evmp_summary)

title: Clinical background
text:
Too few donor hearts are available for the patients who need them, and much recent work in heart transplantation has been about safely using donors and techniques that were once avoided. The studies mapped on this site each followed one of these through the UNOS registry.
In each study, a map showed at a glance where use was concentrated.

title: Clinical background
text:
UNOS regions
The Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network, operated by UNOS, divides the United States into eleven regions, each a group of states, and registry studies often report results by region. The regions mostly follow state lines but not always: Northern Virginia, for example, belongs to Region 2 while the rest of Virginia is in Region 11. The Methodological background page explains how the maps here handle that.

text: This script attaches the packages and defines the constants every other script uses.

title: Setup
text:
Packages
sRtr supplies the region geography and the transplant-center download, so the original scripts’ own data files are no longer needed (Hemmige and Czeresnia 2026). sf handles the spatial data. ggplot2 draws the main version of each map, and tmap (version 4) draws the version with an inset of the Washington-Boston corridor. colorspace provides the OrYel palette the published maps used.


Click to show/hide R Code
library(sRtr)        # UNOS region geography and HRSA transplant centers
library(sf)          # spatial data
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(colorspace)  # sequential "OrYel" palette used in the published maps
library(tmap)        # maps with an inset of the Washington-Boston corridor (tmap 4.x)

title: Setup
text:
Constants

map_crs is the projection every layer is put in before plotting: NAD83 / Conus Albers (EPSG:5070), the projection sRtr stores its region data in.
corridor_extent is the area enlarged in the tmap inset, in longitude and latitude: the Washington-Boston corridor, from DC to Boston, where centers crowd together.
adult_center_exceptions are the two centers with “Children” in their name that the original maps kept because they also transplant adults.
There is no data path: each study’s regional counts are written out in its own script.
label_margin is the gap, in metres, kept between the corridor box and the region numbers placed beside or inside it.
center_label and map_note_template are the legend entry for the center dots and the note printed under every map; {retrieved} in the note becomes the date the HRSA layer was downloaded.
figure_width, figure_height, base_text_size and tiff_dpi size the saved maps for a double-column journal figure: 7 by 4.6 inches, 8-point text, TIFF at 600 dpi.



Click to show/hide R Code
# Projection for every layer: NAD83 / Conus Albers, as in sRtr and HOPE-CDC
map_crs <- 5070

# Extent of the tmap inset, in longitude and latitude: the Washington-Boston
# corridor, where centers crowd together (DC, Baltimore, Philadelphia, New
# York, Hartford, Providence, Boston)
corridor_extent <- c(xmin = -77.6, ymin = 38.6, xmax = -70.5, ymax = 42.9)

# Fill palette and colour for regions with no value
fill_palette <- "OrYel"
missing_fill <- "grey85"

# Organ whose centers are overlaid
center_organ <- "Heart"

# Centers with "Children" in their name that also transplant adults, carried
# over from the original maps (analysis plan section 5)
adult_center_exceptions <- c(
  "Memorial Regional Hospital/Joe DiMaggio Children's Hospital",
  "Providence Sacred Heart Medical Center & Children's Hospital"
)

# Space, in metres, between the corridor box and the region numbers placed
# next to it (main map) or inside it (inset)
label_margin <- 40000

# Legend entry for the center dots, and the note printed under every map.
# {retrieved} is replaced by the date the HRSA layer was downloaded.
center_label <- "Adult heart-transplant center (current HRSA list)"
map_note_template <- str_c(
  "Shading: regional counts from the published study (OPTN/UNOS registry). ",
  "Dots: adult heart-transplant centers in HRSA's current list, retrieved ",
  "{retrieved}; they do not show which centers took part during the study ",
  "period."
)

# Saved maps: 7 inches wide, a double-column journal figure, with text at
# 8 pt. PNG for the website at 300 dpi; PDF (vector) and TIFF at tiff_dpi
# for journal submission.
figure_width <- 7
figure_height <- 4.6
base_text_size <- 8
tiff_dpi <- 600

This page shows where in the United States multiorgan heart transplants from donors after circulatory death (DCD) were done, from Madan et al. (2024), set beside where multiorgan heart transplants of every kind were done. How to read the maps in general is on Reading the maps.

title: DCD donors, 2020–2023
text:
The study in brief
Most donor hearts come from donors after brain death (DBD): the brain has stopped working but the heart is still beating when the organs are recovered. In donation after circulatory death, the heart has stopped before recovery. Hearts from DCD donors have become an important new source of organs, and their use has grown quickly.
The study used the UNOS registry to find the adult multiorgan heart transplants done in the United States from January 2020 to June 2023: 87 with DCD donors (77 heart-kidney, 6 heart-lung and 4 heart-liver) and 1,494 with DBD donors, 1,581 in all. DCD donors rose from 1% of multiorgan heart transplants in the first half of 2020 to 12% in the first half of 2023, with wide variation across UNOS regions and across centers of different size. Six-month survival after heart-kidney transplantation was similar with DCD and DBD donors (Madan et al. 2024). The maps show the regional part of that finding.

title: DCD donors, 2020–2023
text:
What the maps show
There are two maps, both shares of a national count (see Two kinds of percentage):

Share of the country’s DCD-donor multiorgan heart transplants: each region’s number of them divided by 87.
Share of all the country’s multiorgan heart transplants: each region’s number of multiorgan heart transplants with any donor, DCD or DBD, divided by 1,581.

The first shows where DCD-donor transplants were done. The second shows where multiorgan heart transplants were done at all, which is what the first should be read against: a region that does many multiorgan heart transplants will tend to have a large share of the DCD ones too.
The original code also drew a map of each count. Because each share is the count divided by one national total, a count map has exactly the same colours as its share map; only the numbers in the legend differ. This page shows the share maps, the table gives the counts, and the count maps can be downloaded below.

Reading map 1
Three regions did about two thirds of the DCD-donor transplants (57 of 87, 66%): Region 11, from Virginia to Tennessee and the Carolinas, with 23 (26%); Region 5, from California to New Mexico, with 19 (22%); and Region 1, New England, with 15 (17%). Region 1 is small on the map, so look for it in the enlarged corridor of the tmap version.
Two regions did none. Region 2, from Pennsylvania to Washington, DC, and Region 6, the Northwest, did no DCD-donor multiorgan heart transplants in the study period. They are drawn in the lightest colour because their value is zero, not grey, because the value is known. Region 10 did one.
The rest did between 3 and 9: Region 9 (New York and Vermont) did 9, Regions 3 and 7 did 7 each, and Regions 4 and 8 did 3 each.

Reading map 2
Region 5 stands out: it did 374 of the 1,581 multiorgan heart transplants (24%), nearly twice as many as any other region. Regions 11 (211, 13%), 4 (182, 12%) and 9 (179, 11%) come next. The smallest are Region 6 (27, 2%) and Region 8 (38, 2%), and Region 1 (66, 4%).
This map is the background against which map 1 should be read. Its colour scale runs from 2% to 24%; map 1’s runs from 0% to 26%. The colours of the two maps are therefore close but not identical in meaning, so compare them through the numbers.

title: DCD donors, 2020–2023
text:
Comparing the two maps
Setting each region’s share of DCD-donor transplants beside its share of all multiorgan heart transplants shows which regions did more DCD-donor transplants than their size would suggest:

Far more than their size. Region 1 had 17% of the DCD-donor transplants but only 4% of all multiorgan heart transplants, about four times as much: it is pale on map 2 and dark on map 1. Region 11 had about twice as much (26% against 13%).
About in line with their size. Region 5 (22% against 24%), Region 9 (10% against 11%) and Region 3 (8% against 9%). Region 5’s dark colour on map 1 reflects mainly how many multiorgan heart transplants it does.
Far less than their size. Region 4, Texas and Oklahoma, had 12% of all multiorgan heart transplants but 3% of the DCD-donor ones, and Region 10 had 7% and 1%. Region 2 had 6% of all multiorgan heart transplants and none of the DCD-donor ones.
Too few to say. Region 8’s 3 DCD-donor transplants (3%, against 2% of all) and Region 6’s none (against 27 multiorgan heart transplants of any kind) rest on very small numbers.

This comparison is not the same as each region’s own rate of DCD-donor use, which the published maps did not show.

Points to keep in mind

Small numbers. There were 87 DCD-donor multiorgan heart transplants in three and a half years. Eight regions did 9 or fewer, so one or two transplants would change their colour a lot.

title: About

How this website was created
The site is built with Quarto from the scripts themselves. Each code page imports the labelled sections of its script from R/ and shows them with an explanation; the site never runs the analysis.
The repository was set up with the R Analysis Workflow plugin and an AI assistant (Claude), working on branches and through pull requests reviewed by the maintainer.
Four documents describe the project. In short: the plan is the scientific intent, the architecture is the workflow as implemented, and AGENTS.md holds the rules for working together.

Analysis plan: what the maps are meant to show, and why.
Architecture: how the code does it.
AGENTS.md: how people and AI assistants work on the project.
Repository blueprint: the layout every project of this kind starts from.

The project
This is a teaching repository. It reproduces the UNOS-region maps from a series of published heart-transplantation registry studies (HCV donors, DCD donors and ex vivo machine perfusion so far) and shows how to draw them with the sRtr package instead of hand-built region tables, local shapefiles and downloaded center lists. Each study’s regional counts (one row per UNOS region) come from its paper’s analysis of UNOS registry data and are written out in its script. The original RMDs are kept in original/, with local folder paths removed. The code and methods are published as a Quarto website, with one page per study.

analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it. If code needs to depart from the plan, open a decision issue, or comment on the existing one, for the deciders. Once a decider has settled it (in the issue, or relayed there in their exact words), the plan change and the code can go in the same pull request, which closes the issue.
Deciders. Scientific decisions are made by: Shivank Madan (study questions, regional summaries and which measures each map shows) and Vagish Hemmige (mapping methods and code). To be confirmed by both. Anyone may open or contribute to a decision issue; only a decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
This is an analysis project, not an R package. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or pkgdown infrastructure, or apply CRAN conventions.
Default branch: main, protected. Changes reach it only through pull requests.

To allow more for a source, a person changes its row through a pull request, naming the agreement and section that permit it, the approved AI service, and exactly what agents may do. Agents never propose or make this change themselves, and nothing in personal instructions can grant it.
For every package:

Read its documentation before writing code for a source, including known issues. Behavior that sets the cohort, an exposure, an outcome, or a denominator is checked in the documentation, not assumed from a function’s name.

For packages this team maintains:

Facts about the source belong in the package’s documentation, not in this file. If the package lacks something this project needs to know, add it there or open an issue there.
Problems belong in the package. If a function is wrong or does not quite do what the plan needs, open an issue in its repository. Fix it in the package (preferred when generally useful) or wrap it here with a code comment linking the issue, and remove the wrapper once the issue is fixed.

For external packages:

Work around problems here. Wrap the function in R/functions.R with a comment explaining the problem and linking any upstream issue. Reporting a bug upstream is an external communication; the person directing the work decides whether to file it.
Facts about the source that this project relies on (definitions, release quirks, suppression rules) go in references/ with a citation to the provider’s documentation, or in the plan when they shape a decision.

For a source with no package: one loading script records the download URL, the release or access date, and any processing. Verify its variables against the provider’s documentation for that release.

Exploration and definitive analysis
Exploration is welcome on branches or forks. Experimental scripts need not be sourced from R/main.R or have Quarto pages, and their findings are labelled preliminary. A script becomes part of the definitive analysis when it is sourced from R/main.R; from then on every rule below applies to it.

R scripts

Running the analysis. Run R/main.R from the project root. It sources the other scripts in dependency order; ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each does.
One job per script. When you add a definitive script, source it from main.R at the right point and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request.
Header comment. Each script begins with what it does, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, and what it produces.
Constants, libraries, and code lists live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code values. Any number a reader might want to change (a window, a year, a threshold, a ratio) is a named constant there.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects.
No side effects outside the project. No setwd(), absolute paths, or writes outside the project. Restricted data are located only through their access package’s configuration.
No results in the repository. No script (exploratory or definitive) or comment, commit message, issue, pull-request text or review report contains results, counts or data values from restricted data unless they are cleared for release. Check before every commit and post, since a public repository publishes everything pushed to it, on any branch.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections so Quarto pages can show the code without copying it:
## ---- <step-name>

Every logical step has a label. A label covers the code from its line to the next label.
Labels are kebab-case, describe the step, and are unique across all scripts; a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code.
Search the .qmd files before renaming or deleting a label.
Labels are comments and never change what the code does.

Variable labels
Label analysis variables with human-readable descriptions (for example labelled::set_variable_labels(), or the access package’s labelling functions where it has them). Label each derived variable where it is created, with units, price year, and windows where they apply.

Quarto website
The site documents the code. It does not run the analysis.

_quarto.yml, index.qmd, 404.qmd (the page GitHub Pages shows for a missing address) and styles.css sit at the root; quarto/ has one page per definitive script, named after it, plus the Background, Study design and methods, About and project-document pages. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode, Results and Pending callouts.
Visual cues. Each kind of page has one sidebar icon, coloured by styles.css, and pages mark the same kind of content with the callout of that colour: background book (blue); study design and methods diagram-3 (orange); R code laptop (pink, Rcode 💻); results clipboard-data (green, Results 📊); project documents file-earmark-ruled (grey). Give every new page the icon of its kind.
Provisional content. quarto/_pending.lua highlights in yellow every paragraph that starts with Decision pending: or, in the plan, Open:, and any [text]{.pending}, and adds a ⏳ Pending callout to pages that have a mark. Mark only what an open decision could change, and remove the mark when the decision is settled.
Project documents. analysis-plan.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md and REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md are shown on the site by pages in quarto/ that only include the root file, which stays the one source: edit the root file, not the page.
Each page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. Pages render without restricted data. Only the read_chunk() imports, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md, site helpers that read code or text, and the results pages’ chunk that reads tables/ run.
Publishing route: a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml) draws the maps with R/main.R, renders the site and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. It runs on every push to main and by hand; on a pull request it only draws and renders, as a check. docs/ is the local render output and is not committed. When you add a script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update its explanation in the same pull request.

Outputs

Tables and figures are exported by R/tables.R and R/figures.R to tables/ and figures/. Maps are saved by each study script to figures/<study>/ as PNG, PDF and 600 dpi TIFF, and each study’s regional table to tables/<study>_regions.csv. The maps show values already published in the papers, so they are public, but figures/ and tables/ are not committed: the publish workflow redraws them on every run, where the live HRSA download works, and they go out with the site. The Results pages (quarto/results.qmd on how to read the maps, then quarto/results_<study>.qmd, one per study) show the maps and tables and link the PDFs; each workflow run keeps all the files, TIFFs included, as an artifact. Maps drawn from synthetic values are not results, are never described as results, and are not committed to figures/.
Published figures need alt text.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)
The Access column of “Data sources” says which sources are restricted. For each restricted source:

Never commit data, extracts, or saved objects or outputs derived from patient-level records. Keep data outside the repository, and check .gitignore before adding a new output type.
AI agents never read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents do not open data files or patient-level objects, print rows, or display identifiers, person-level dates, or small geographies. Agents also do not open outputs from restricted data that are not yet cleared for release (for example tables/ and figures/ while they are ignored). Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data; results on real data are produced by an authorized person. The only exception is what the Data sources table explicitly allows for a source, and only within those words.
Synthetic data are built in code, labelled as synthetic, and never derived from real records.
Disclosure. This project uses no restricted source: the regional summaries are published region-level values. If a study is added whose regional values are not published, its row in Data sources starts as restricted and these rules apply to it. Check every output before it leaves the approved environment, including scripts, comments, commit messages, issues, pull-request text and review reports (see R scripts).
Credentials and paid APIs. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron. Ask before paid, bulk, or uncached API calls. Before a paid batch, make one call with the exact package version, model and settings, and check the result before running the rest. Which model or service version to use is the person’s choice; an agent proposes, with the cost if known, and does not switch it on its own.

Coding conventions

Cohort flow (not used here: this project draws no cohort) uses the flowchart package, so the STROBE flow diagram and the analytic cohort come from the same code. Every inclusion or exclusion goes through fc_filter(), in the plan’s order. Never remove people from the cohort outside the flowchart. Record-level processing (cleaning claims, choosing among a person’s records) is fine. An analysis that uses fewer people than the cohort (complete cases, a subgroup) reports its own number with that analysis. The cohort used downstream is the data from the final step (fc_view(what = "data")). Flowchart labels are built from constants in setup.R.
Code lists carry each code’s category, code system and version, and matching rule (exact or prefix). Check every code against the official code set. Never invent codes, variables, files, or definitions.
Joins use join_by() with an explicit relationship where possible. After every interval join and every join of records to people, assert that rows did not multiply, and decide deliberately what happens to unmatched rows.
Dates and windows are written as inclusive offsets from the index date, matching the plan, and the edges are tested on synthetic data.
Code that turns model output into reported numbers lives in named functions in R/functions.R, tested on synthetic data with a known answer.
Package APIs: read the help page and NEWS for the installed version before calling a package; don’t write calls from memory. A test that fakes a package checks only our own logic, so call the real package once (synthetic data, or one cheap call) before relying on the code.
Style: readable for a clinician-analyst who learned R from online guides: pipes and dplyr/tidyr verbs, case_when(), loops over names or named lists rather than the apply family, Reduce or positional indexing. Required base R goes in a named, tested function. Tidyverse layout; style changes in their own commits.

Checks for any change
Check the items that apply before opening a pull request.

Plan: does the change implement the plan as written, and does it leave every open decision open?
Data sources: does it use the access package’s functions, and does their documented behavior match what the plan needs?
Package APIs: for new or changed calls to a package, does the pull request name the installed version and the help page or NEWS entry relied on?
Cohort: do the flowchart steps’ order, denominators, and labels match their conditions, and can each count be reproduced from code?
Joins and denominators: no unintended row multiplication; missing, suppressed, and zero kept distinct.
Reported numbers: does each estimate match the plan’s estimand, and do tables, figures, and site prose say what the code actually computes?
Structure: is ARCHITECTURE.md current; are chunk labels unique and found by their pages; does every definitive script have a page and sidebar entry; does any site chunk run analysis code? Only the hidden read_chunk() imports, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md, site helpers that read code or text, and results pages reading outputs cleared for release, run.
Disclosure: search every changed tracked file, and the commit messages and pull-request text, for dates, record IDs, names, absolute paths and numbers that could come from restricted data. Read each hit in context; legitimate ones (plan dates, deciders’ names, synthetic examples) stay.
Execution: does main.R run in a fresh session with relative paths; are any saved intermediates or caches stale?
Geography: every layer is in map_crs (EPSG:5070) before plotting; the regional summary matches all eleven regions; centers are one row per OTC_CD; center points are drawn at their true locations (no jitter).
Original code: files in original/ are the provenance of each map and are not edited, except that paths on anyone’s computer are removed before they are committed. No tracked file contains a local path.

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent sets its working style (review only, step by step, or hands-off) in their own instructions, and may add stricter rules; those take precedence. Without a style, an agent works step by step. At most, an agent may edit code and documentation, add scripts and tests, run code and render the site on synthetic data, and commit to a branch and open a pull request.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to a decision issue. A decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; asks before running the full pipeline or making expensive calls; shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this; and proposes another way of writing something already agreed before committing it.
Pull requests opened by an agent are focused. Each says which plan section or issue it addresses, what was checked, and whether by running code on synthetic data or by reading only. Synthetic results are never described as results.
References: cite the source documentation and literature used, in references.bib.
Project documentsRepository blueprint Code

Analytical scripts

R/main.R sources definitive scripts in dependency order.
Typical workflow: setup → cohort construction → processing → modeling → outputs.
Study-specific scripts may be grouped into subdirectories by analytical stage.
R/tables.R and R/figures.R may generate outputs directly or orchestrate specialized scripts.

Documentation

Document definitive analytical scripts with explanatory Quarto pages; exploratory scripts need not have pages.
Use Cryptococcus-cost-analysis as an example for Quarto supporting files, chunk imports, callouts, and formatting—not scientific methods.
Quarto source and rendered output locations may vary by project.

Outputs and version control

Track approved, nonrestricted outputs when useful for publication; otherwise retain them locally and exclude them from Git.
.gitignore: Exclude restricted data, credentials, caches, temporary files, and generated outputs unless intentionally tracked (e.g., .Rproj.user/, .Rhistory, .RData, .httr-oauth, .quarto/, cache/, figures/, tables/, *.quarto_ipynb); verify exclusions cover actual output paths without hiding necessary source or reference files.

This script draws the regional maps for the study of multiorgan heart transplantation with hepatitis C virus (HCV) donors, August 2015 to August 2020, which reported wide variation in HCV-donor use across UNOS regions (Madan et al. 2021).

title: 2. HCV donors (2021)
text:
Regional summary
The original map read these counts from a spreadsheet, UNOS regions.xlsx. With eleven rows they fit in the script itself, written out with tribble(), a table laid out row by row. The totals are the paper’s: 109 multiorgan heart transplants with HCV donors out of 1,322. The map shows each region’s share of the 109, which is what the spreadsheet’s Percentage_HT_HCV held.
Only the counts are typed in; the percentages are computed from them, so how each is defined can be read in the code. The join to the map stops if any of the eleven regions is missing.

Decision pending: a share of the national count is highest where the most transplants are done, so it shows where HCV-donor transplants happened rather than how often each region used HCV donors. Whether to add a map of each region’s own rate (n_hcv / n_total) is decision D3 in SETUP-NOTES.md.



Click to show/hide R Code
# Multiorgan heart transplants by UNOS region, August 2015 to August 2020:
# those using HCV donors, and all of them. The totals (109 and 1,322) are the
# paper's. Percentages are each region's share of the national count, as in
# the regional spreadsheet the original map read.
hcv_summary <- tibble::tribble(
  ~region,     ~n_hcv, ~n_total,
  "Region 1",      10,       53,
  "Region 2",       6,      107,
  "Region 3",       5,      125,
  "Region 4",       2,      143,
  "Region 5",      15,      358,
  "Region 6",       4,       20,
  "Region 7",       4,      143,
  "Region 8",       1,       33,
  "Region 9",      17,       91,
  "Region 10",     14,       95,
  "Region 11",     31,      154
) |>
  mutate(
    pct_of_us_hcv = 100 * n_hcv / sum(n_hcv),
    pct_of_us_total = 100 * n_total / sum(n_total)
  )

hcv_measures <- c(
  pct_of_us_hcv = "Share of U.S. HCV-donor\nmultiorgan HTs (%)"
)

hcv_states <- join_region_values(region_states, hcv_summary)

title: Overview
text: A series of heart-transplantation studies from Montefiore and Albert Einstein College of Medicine used the UNOS registry to follow how new kinds of donors and new technologies entered practice: hepatitis C virus (HCV) donors in multiorgan transplantation (Madan et al. 2021), donation after circulatory death (DCD) donors (Madan et al. 2024) and ex vivo machine perfusion of donor hearts (Madan et al. 2025). Each found that uptake varied widely across the eleven UNOS regions, and each showed that variation with a map. More on the clinical background page.

title: Overview
text:
What this site does
It reproduces each study’s regional map, and teaches how to draw it with the sRtr package. The original maps were built from a hand-split region table, a local Census shapefile, a hand-entered sheet of label positions and a downloaded list of transplant centers. sRtr holds the region geography and downloads the current HRSA transplant-center layer, so each map now takes a few package calls. Every layer is projected to NAD83 / Conus Albers before plotting, and each map is drawn twice: once with ggplot2, and once with tmap with the crowded Washington-Boston corridor enlarged in an inset.

title: Overview
text:
Methods
Each study’s regional summary, one row per region, is joined to sRtr’s state polygons and shaded by region. Study design and methods explains each choice, and the authoritative specification is the analysis plan. The original code is on Original RMDs.

title: HCV donors, 2015–2020
text:
The study in brief
Organs from donors with HCV were once rarely used, because the infection could pass to the recipient. Effective antiviral treatment made it possible to use them, adding to the small supply of organs for patients who need a heart and a second organ (see Clinical background).
The study used the UNOS registry to find all 1,322 adult multiorgan heart transplants done in the United States between August 2015 and August 2020: 986 heart-kidney, 155 heart-lung and 181 heart-liver. Of these, 109 used HCV donors. HCV donor here includes two groups: 77 donors with virus in the blood (positive on nucleic acid amplification testing, NAT, called viremic) and 32 with antibodies but no virus (antibody-positive, NAT-negative, nonviremic).
The share of multiorgan heart transplants using HCV donors rose from none in 2015 to 14% in 2020, with wide variation across UNOS regions and across centers of different size. One-year survival after heart-kidney transplantation was similar with HCV donors and with donors who had never had HCV (Madan et al. 2021). The map shows the regional part of that finding.

title: HCV donors, 2015–2020
text:
What the map shows
Each region is shaded by its share of the country’s HCV-donor multiorgan heart transplants: its number of them divided by 109, the national total. The eleven shares add up to 100%.
This is a share of the national count, not the region’s own rate (see Two kinds of percentage). It shows where in the country the 109 transplants were done. It does not show how often each region chose an HCV donor when it did a multiorgan heart transplant.

title: HCV donors, 2015–2020
text:
Reading this map
The darkest region is Region 11, the band from Virginia through Kentucky, Tennessee and the Carolinas. It did 31 of the 109 transplants (28%), more than a quarter of the country’s total.
Three more regions are mid-to-dark: Region 9, mostly New York State, with 17 (16%); Region 5, from California to New Mexico, with 15 (14%); and Region 10, Indiana, Michigan and Ohio, with 14 (13%). Together with Region 11, these four regions did 77 of the 109 (71%).
The lightest regions are Region 8 in the central Plains, with 1 transplant (under 1%), and Region 4, Texas and Oklahoma, with 2 (2%). Regions 6 and 7 each did 4 (4%).
In the tmap version, the enlarged corridor shows that Regions 1, 2 and 9 meet in the crowded Northeast. Region 1, New England, did 10 (9%), and Region 2, from Pennsylvania to Washington, DC, did 6 (6%).

title: HCV donors, 2015–2020
section: Compared with all multiorgan heart transplants
text:
Compared with all multiorgan heart transplants
A busy region tends to have a large share of any kind of transplant, so the map partly reflects how many multiorgan heart transplants each region did of any kind. The table below gives each region’s share of all 1,322 as well. Setting the two shares side by side shows which regions did more HCV-donor transplants than their size alone would suggest:

More than their size would suggest. Region 11 had 28% of the HCV-donor transplants but 12% of all multiorgan heart transplants, more than twice as much. Region 9 (16% against 7%) and Region 1 (9% against 4%) were also more than twice their overall share, and Region 10 nearly twice (13% against 7%).
Less than their size would suggest. Region 5 did the most multiorgan heart transplants of any region (27% of all of them) but only 14% of those with HCV donors, about half. Region 4 had 11% of all multiorgan heart transplants and 2% of those with HCV donors, and Region 7 had 11% and 4%.
Too few to say. Region 6 had 4% of the HCV-donor transplants and 2% of all multiorgan heart transplants, which looks like a high ratio, but it rests on 4 HCV-donor transplants out of 20.

This comparison is not the same as each region’s own rate of HCV-donor use, which the published map did not show.

Decision pending: whether to add a map of each region’s own rate, its HCV-donor transplants divided by its own multiorgan heart transplants, labelled as not in the paper (D3 in SETUP-NOTES.md).

Small numbers. Seven of the eleven regions did 10 or fewer HCV-donor multiorgan heart transplants in five years, and Region 8 did one. In those regions, one or two transplants more or fewer would change the colour a lot.

text:
The map, in ggplot2
This replaces the original maps’ geom_sf() calls with several changes. The plot is drawn in map_crs (coord_sf(crs = ...)) rather than in longitude and latitude, so the country is not stretched east to west. Centers are drawn with geom_sf() at their true locations; the original geom_jitter() moved each point randomly by up to 0.3 degrees, which is about 30 km. Mapping the centers’ shape to center_label gives them their own legend entry. Region numbers sit on a pale box (geom_sf_label()) so they read on any fill colour. The note in the caption says what the shading and the dots are, so a figure taken off this site still explains itself. Text is sized from base_size, in points.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Map one measure: states shaded by region value, region outlines on top,
# region numbers on a pale box so they read on any fill, transplant centers
# at their true locations with their own legend entry, and a note saying
# what the shading and the dots are.
map_regions_ggplot <- function(region_states, region_outlines, region_labels,
                               fill_var, legend_title, centers, center_label,
                               note, palette, na_fill, crs, base_size) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(
      data = region_states,
      mapping = aes(fill = .data[[fill_var]]),
      colour = "grey55",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ) +
    geom_sf(data = region_outlines, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_sf(
      data = centers,
      mapping = aes(shape = center_label),
      size = 1,
      alpha = 0.6
    ) +
    geom_sf_label(
      data = region_labels,
      mapping = aes(label = label),
      colour = "navy",
      fill = alpha("white", 0.75),
      fontface = "bold",
      size = base_size / .pt
    ) +
    scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = palette, na.value = na_fill) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = 16, name = NULL) +
    coord_sf(crs = crs, datum = NA) +
    labs(fill = legend_title, caption = str_wrap(note, 110)) +
    theme_void(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = base_size * 0.8),
      legend.position = "right"
    )
}

title: Functions
section: The map, in tmap, with a corridor inset
text:
The map, in tmap, with a corridor inset
Between Washington and Boston, transplant centers crowd so closely that they overlap on a national map. The map’s layers are written once, in map_layers(), and used twice: for the main map and, with bbox set to the corridor, for the inset. Building the inset as its own map, rather than giving tm_inset() a bounding box, lets it carry its own region numbers (inset_labels); a red outline of corridor_box on the main map shows where it is. tm_pos_out() places the inset outside the map frame, to the right, and the colour legend, the center symbol (tm_add_legend()) and the note (tm_credits()) along the bottom, so none of them hides any part of the country. One difference from ggplot2: tmap takes the palette as a vector of colours, which has to be reversed (rev = TRUE) so that high values get the dark end, as they do in scale_fill_continuous_sequential().


Click to show/hide R Code
# The same map in tmap, with the Washington-Boston corridor enlarged in an
# inset beside it. The inset is drawn as its own map, so it carries its own
# region numbers, and a red box on the main map shows where it is. The legend,
# the center symbol and the note run along the bottom.
map_regions_tmap <- function(region_states, region_outlines, main_labels,
                             inset_labels, fill_var, legend_title, centers,
                             center_label, inset_box, note, palette, na_fill) {
  # rev = TRUE puts the dark end of the palette on high values, matching
  # scale_fill_continuous_sequential() in the ggplot2 maps
  fill_scale <- tm_scale_continuous(
    values = sequential_hcl(7, palette = palette, rev = TRUE),
    value.na = na_fill
  )

  # The layers shared by the main map and the inset
  map_layers <- function(labels, bbox, fill_legend) {
    tm_shape(region_states, bbox = bbox) +
      tm_polygons(
        fill = fill_var,
        fill.scale = fill_scale,
        fill.legend = fill_legend,
        col = "grey55",
        lwd = 0.5
      ) +
      tm_shape(region_outlines) +
      tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 1) +
      tm_shape(centers) +
      tm_dots(size = 0.15, fill_alpha = 0.6) +
      tm_shape(labels) +
      tm_text(
        "label",
        col = "navy",
        fontface = "bold",
        size = 0.55,
        bgcol = "white",
        bgcol_alpha = 0.75
      )
  }

  corridor_map <- map_layers(inset_labels, st_bbox(inset_box), tm_legend_hide())

  map_layers(
    main_labels,
    NULL,
    tm_legend(
      title = legend_title,
      orientation = "landscape",
      position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom")
    )
  ) +
    tm_shape(inset_box) +
    tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 1) +
    # Outside the map frame, to the right, so it hides nothing on the map
    tm_inset(
      corridor_map,
      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"),
      width = 16,
      height = 16,
      frame = FALSE
    ) +
    tm_add_legend(
      type = "symbols",
      labels = center_label,
      fill = "black",
      size = 0.4,
      position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom")
    ) +
    tm_credits(
      str_wrap(note, 105),
      position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom"),
      size = 0.6
    ) +
    tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
}

Which states are in each region
The Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN), operated by the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS), groups the states into eleven regions. The maps use the grouping in sRtr’s region table, which places each state in one region. Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico are not on the maps.

The regions differ a great deal in size and in how many transplants they do. Region 6 covers four large states in the Northwest but does few transplants; Region 9 is mostly New York State; Region 5 includes California and does the most multiorgan heart transplants of any region. A region’s colour says nothing about its area, but a large region catches the eye, so read the legend and the table rather than the amount of colour.
The Clinical background page says more about the regions, and Methodological background explains how a region that crosses a state line is handled.

title: Reading the maps
text:
Two kinds of percentage
The maps use two different percentages, and they answer different questions. The legend of every map says which one it shows.






Share of the national count, or the region's own rate



A region’s share of the national count is the region’s transplants of one kind divided by all such transplants in the United States. The eleven shares add up to 100%. The HCV and DCD maps show this. It answers the question where in the country were these transplants done?
A region’s own rate is the region’s transplants of one kind divided by the region’s own transplants. The rates do not add up to anything. The machine-perfusion map shows this. It answers the question how often did this region use the technique?


The two can tell different stories about the same region. A worked example from the machine-perfusion study: Region 11 did 129 of the country’s 561 machine-perfusion transplants, the largest share of any region (23%). But it also did many transplants overall, so only 129 of its 1,687 DBD heart transplants (8%) used machine perfusion. Region 1 did fewer machine-perfusion transplants (79, a 14% share), but they were 79 of only 577 transplants, so its own rate (14%) was the highest in the country (Madan et al. 2025).
The general rule: a region that does many transplants of every kind tends to have a large share of any one kind. A high share of the national count is therefore partly a sign of a busy region. To see whether a region used a donor type more than its size would predict, compare its share of that donor type with its share of all transplants. The HCV and DCD tables give both, and their pages make that comparison.

Decision pending: whether to add maps of each region’s own rate for the HCV and DCD studies, beside the published share maps (D3 in SETUP-NOTES.md).

title: Reading the maps
section: Each map has its own colour scale
text:
Each map has its own colour scale
The colour scale of each map runs from that map’s lowest value to its highest. Dark red on the HCV map means about 28%; on the machine-perfusion map it means about 14%. Colours cannot be compared from one map to another, only within a map. To compare across maps, read the legends or the tables.

title: Reading the maps
section: What the maps cannot tell you
text:
What the maps cannot tell you

Nothing about a single state. The whole region carries one value. A dark state may have done none of the region’s transplants; a neighbouring state in the same region may have done all of them.
Not why regions differ. The studies described variation; they did not test what caused it. Differences may reflect a few centers’ practice, local donor supply, distances, or chance where numbers are small.
Not which centers took part. The dots are adult heart-transplant centers in HRSA’s list on the day the maps were drawn, not the centers that existed during each study period, and not the centers that did the transplants mapped. A center that opened after a study ended still has a dot; one that closed has none. This was decided for the teaching purpose of the maps (D1 in SETUP-NOTES.md; plan §4).
Not how many transplants a center did. Every dot is the same size. A region with many dots does not necessarily do many transplants.
Not how certain the values are. Where a region did only a few transplants of a kind, one or two more or fewer would change its colour a lot. The tables give the counts so this can be judged.

The paper behind each map gives the full analysis, including trends over time and patient outcomes, which a regional map cannot show.

title: Study design and methods
text:
What is mapped
Each study’s paper computed a few summaries for every UNOS region: how many transplants used a donor type or technology, and what percentage that was. The maps show those summaries as published; nothing new is estimated. Every state in a region is shaded with the region’s value.
Specified in: §2 Objectives, §6 Estimation.
The HCV and DCD percentages are each region’s share of the national count; the machine-perfusion percentage is each region’s own rate. The legends say which.

text:
Where the geography comes from
The region assignment of each state and the region outlines come from sRtr, built from the same Census boundaries and region table the original maps used. Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico are left out, as in the original maps.
Specified in: §4 Data sources, §5 Study populations and unit definitions.

Which transplant centers are shown

How the maps are drawn
Every layer is projected to NAD83 / Conus Albers, and each map is drawn twice: with ggplot2, matching the published maps’ look, and with tmap, adding an inset that enlarges the Washington-Boston corridor.
Specified in: §2, §7 Linkage and geography.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Publication of the regional values
The regional counts are published in each paper, so they are written out in the code and the maps are public.
Specified in: §12 Disclosure control.
Project documentsAnalysis plan Code

Scope and reporting framework
This document is the authoritative specification of the study’s scientific objectives, population, definitions, estimands and statistical methods. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the implementation, AGENTS.md the working conventions, and GitHub Issues the open decisions and implementation status. Neither file supersedes this plan.
This repository reproduces the regional maps from a series of published heart-transplantation studies that used the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry, and teaches how to build them with the sRtr package (Hemmige and Czeresnia 2026). The underlying studies, their cohorts and their regional summaries are specified in the published papers; this plan covers only how a regional summary becomes a map. Reporting follows STROBE and RECORD (Elm et al. 2007; Benchimol et al. 2015) as they apply to a descriptive figure. The reporting map below links each checklist item to a section of this plan.

1. Background and rationale
Each study below reported that use of a donor type or technology varied widely across UNOS regions. A map of the eleven UNOS regions shows that variation at a glance. The original maps were drawn with hand-built region tables, a local Census shapefile and a downloaded list of transplant centers. The sRtr package now holds the region geography and downloads the transplant-center layer, so the same maps can be drawn from a few package calls.

2. Objectives

Primary: for each study, draw a map of the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia, with each state shaded by the value of its UNOS region and the eleven region boundaries drawn over the states.
Secondary: overlay the locations of adult heart-transplant centers on the same map.
Teaching: show the original code and the sRtr version side by side for each study.








Study
Measures mapped by region




HCV donors in multiorgan heart transplantation, 2015–2020 (Madan et al. 2021)
Region’s share of all U.S. multiorgan HTs with HCV donors (of 109)


DCD donors in multiorgan heart transplantation, 2020–2023 (Madan et al. 2024)
Number of multiorgan HTs with DCD donors, and the region’s share of them (of 87); number of all multiorgan HTs, and the region’s share of them (of 1,581)


Ex vivo machine perfusion in DBD heart transplantation, 2020–2024 (Madan et al. 2025)
Share of the region’s own DBD HTs using ex vivo machine perfusion




Open: whether the HCV and DCD maps should also show each region’s own rate (its HCV- or DCD-donor transplants as a share of its own multiorgan transplants), since a share of the national count largely follows regional volume (decision D3 in SETUP-NOTES.md; issue to be filed).

The COVID-19 donor study (Madan et al. 2023) and the donor offer acceptance study (Ramineni et al. 2026) join this table when their mapping code is added.

3. Study design and setting
Descriptive mapping of region-level summaries already computed for each published study. No new cohort is drawn and no new statistic is estimated.

4. Data sources and measurement periods

Regional counts: for each study, the number of transplants by UNOS region, written out in that study’s script. They are the counts behind the published regional figures, and their totals match the papers (109 of 1,322; 87 of 1,581; 561 of 12,363) (Madan et al. 2021, 2024, 2025). Each was computed from the UNOS registry for the study period above.
Region geography: UNOS_regions_sf from sRtr, state polygons from the 2018 Census cartographic boundary file (1:20,000,000) with each state’s UNOS region (Hemmige and Czeresnia 2026).
Transplant centers: the HRSA organ procurement and transplantation layer, downloaded with sRtr::get_hrsa_transplant_centers() (Health Resources and Services Administration, n.d.). The original maps used a downloaded copy of an HRSA transplant-center file.

The maps use the current HRSA layer, downloaded each time the code runs. It describes centers as of the day it is downloaded, not as of each study period, so a center that opened or closed since a study period may be shown wrongly; this is accepted because the maps teach the method rather than restate each paper’s center list (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 2026-11-09; recorded in SETUP-NOTES.md, D1).

5. Study populations and unit definitions

Unit of display: the UNOS region. Every state in a region carries that region’s value.
Geography: the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia. Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico are excluded, as in the original maps.
Transplant centers: centers that list heart transplantation, excluding pediatric centers. The original code excluded centers whose name contains “Children”, except Memorial Regional Hospital/Joe DiMaggio Children’s Hospital and Providence Sacred Heart Medical Center & Children’s Hospital, which also transplant adults.


Open: whether to keep the name-based pediatric exclusion with the HRSA layer, whose center names and service lists may differ from the original file (decision D2 in SETUP-NOTES.md; issue to be filed).

6. Estimation
None beyond arithmetic. Percentages are computed from the published counts: for the HCV and DCD studies, each region’s count divided by the national total; for the machine-perfusion study, each region’s EVMP count divided by its own DBD count.

7. Linkage and geography
Regional counts join to UNOS_regions_sf by region name (“Region 1” to “Region 11”). A join that does not match all eleven regions stops the script.

8. Measures and outcomes
As listed for each study in §2.

9. Analysis and interpretation
The maps are descriptive. They show where use of a donor type or technology was higher or lower; they do not estimate why, and a shaded state says nothing about that state alone, only about its region.

10. Missing data and validity requirements
A region with no value is drawn in grey and named in the legend as having no data, not as zero.

11. Sensitivity analyses
None.

12. Disclosure control
Each regional summary holds region-level values that are published in its paper (Madan et al. 2021, 2024, 2025). The counts and the maps drawn from them are therefore public, as stated by Vagish Hemmige on 2026-11-09 (recorded in SETUP-NOTES.md). No patient-level data are used.

13. Limitations to address in reporting

Shading whole states by region hides variation within a region.
Center locations show where programs are, not how many transplants each performed.

title: 1. Map geography

States and regions
In the original scripts this took three files: a spreadsheet listing each region’s states, the 2018 Census state shapefile, and code to split, pivot and join them. sRtr was built from exactly that code, so the result now ships with the package as UNOS_regions_sf: one row per state (the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia) with its region. get_hrsa_optn_regions() dissolves the states into one outline per region. Both are put in map_crs, so every layer shares one projection.

The original maps used a copy of an HRSA transplant-center file downloaded once. get_hrsa_transplant_centers() downloads the current layer from HRSA each time it runs (Health Resources and Services Administration, n.d.), which is then narrowed to adult heart centers (see Functions).
The layer shows centers as they are on the day the code runs, not as they were during each study period, so a center that has since opened or closed may be shown wrongly. That is accepted here because the maps teach the method (plan §4). The download date is recorded, and goes into the note printed under every map, so a figure that leaves this site still says which list its dots come from and that they are not the study period’s centers.

    adult_exceptions = adult_center_exceptions,

Region numbers
Each region’s number sits on a point from st_point_on_surface(), which is guaranteed to fall inside the region; a centroid can fall outside a region whose shape is irregular. These points replace the hand-entered label positions the original maps read from a spreadsheet.
The corridor inset needs two sets of points, made by place_region_labels() (see Functions). main_labels keeps every number clear of the red box on the main map. inset_labels gives every region that appears in the enlarged view its own number there: Regions 1, 2, 9 and 11.

title: Methodological background
text: A short introduction to drawing maps in R, enough to follow the code on this site. For a fuller treatment, Kyle Walker’s Analyzing US Census Data is free online (Walker 2023). Its chapters on Census geographic data, mapping and spatial analysis cover everything here in more depth, with US examples. The links below point to the relevant sections.

title: Methodological background
section: Spatial data are data frames with a geometry column
text:
Spatial data are data frames with a geometry column
The sf package stores spatial data as an ordinary data frame with one extra column, geometry, holding a point, line or polygon for each row. So the usual dplyr verbs work on it: filter() keeps some regions, left_join() attaches a table of values, and group_by() with summarise() merges polygons, which is how states become regions. Walker introduces sf objects in §5.1.1.
On this site, sRtr supplies the sf objects: UNOS_regions_sf (one polygon per state, tagged with its UNOS region), get_hrsa_optn_regions() (one polygon per region) and get_hrsa_transplant_centers() (one point per center and organ) (Hemmige and Czeresnia 2026). Walker uses the tigris package for Census boundaries in the same way; sRtr’s state polygons come from the same Census cartographic boundary files.

title: Methodological background
text:
Coordinate reference systems
Every geometry is stored in a coordinate reference system (CRS). Longitude and latitude are angles, not distances; drawn as if they were x and y, they stretch the United States east to west and make northern states look larger than they are. A projected CRS such as NAD83 / Conus Albers (EPSG:5070) is designed for the contiguous states and keeps areas comparable, which matters when the eye reads shaded area.
Two habits follow. Transform every layer to the one CRS with sf::st_transform() before combining or plotting them, as the HOPE-CDC analysis does, rather than relying on the plotting function to reconcile them. And set the CRS of the plot itself with coord_sf(crs = ...). Walker covers both, and how to choose a projection with the crsuggest package, in §5.4.

title: Methodological background
section: A choropleth: shading areas by a value
text:
A choropleth: shading areas by a value
A choropleth shades each area by a value. In ggplot2, geom_sf(aes(fill = value)) draws it; a sequential colour scale suits a quantity that runs from low to high. Walker builds one step by step in §6.2, including the theme_void() and labs() calls used here.
When the value belongs to a UNOS region, every state in the region is shaded the same. Thin state lines under thick region outlines remind the reader of that: the shading says nothing about any state alone. Several UNOS regions also cross state lines (Northern Virginia is in Region 2, for example); sRtr assigns each state to one region, so the map is an approximation at those edges.

title: Methodological background
text:
Points on the map
Transplant centers are points. Drawn with geom_sf() at their true locations, partly transparent, they show where programs are and where they cluster. The original maps used geom_jitter(), which separates overlapping points by moving each one randomly, so no center is where it should be.

title: Methodological background
text:
tmap and insets
tmap is a second mapping package, built for thematic maps; Walker introduces it in §6.3. His examples use tmap 3. This site uses tmap 4, whose syntax changed: tm_polygons(fill = ...) with fill.scale and fill.legend replaces arguments such as col, style and palette. The tmap website documents version 4.
An inset repeats part of the map at a larger scale beside it. Between Washington and Boston, transplant centers sit so close together that they overlap on a national map; tmap’s tm_inset() draws that corridor enlarged. For a related problem, fitting Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico onto a national map, Walker shows tigris’s shift_geometry() in §5.5.1; the maps here leave those places out, as the published maps did.

The ggplot2 version of a region map, drawn from synthetic values, not study results, with synthetic center locations. The centers between Washington and Boston crowd together, which is what the tmap inset addresses.
Project documentsArchitecture Code

Overview
R/main.R runs six scripts in order. The first two set up packages, constants and helper functions. R/map_geography.R builds the map layers every study shares, from the sRtr package and the live HRSA transplant-center layer. Each study script then holds that study’s regional counts, joins them to the shared layers, and saves two maps per measure to figures/<study>/ (one drawn with ggplot2, and one with tmap with an inset of the Washington-Boston corridor), each as PNG, PDF and TIFF, plus a regional table to tables/.
The Quarto website explains the scripts. Its pages import the scripts’ labelled sections with knitr::read_chunk() and show them; they never run the analysis. The Results pages (quarto/results.qmd and one quarto/results_<study>.qmd per study) show the saved maps and tables. A GitHub Actions workflow runs R/main.R, renders the site and publishes it on every push to main, so the maps and the site are always drawn from the code on main.

Publish workflow
Purpose: draws the maps with R/main.R, renders the site and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves.

It installs sRtr from GitHub and the other packages from CRAN, and needs internet access to the HRSA server. Each run keeps figures/ and tables/, TIFFs included, as a downloadable artifact. A failed run publishes nothing, so the last good site stays live.


Provenance
original/ holds the RMDs that drew the published maps, with local paths removed. data/hrsa/Transplant centers.csv is the HRSA file those maps used; the code does not read it, but it is kept for provenance and for checking the pediatric-center rule (decision D2 in SETUP-NOTES.md).

Data flow

R/setup.R attaches packages and sets constants; R/functions.R defines the helpers.
R/map_geography.R takes the state polygons and region outlines from sRtr, downloads the HRSA center layer, narrows it to adult heart centers, and projects every layer to EPSG:5070.
Each study script builds its regional table from counts written in the script, computes percentages (shares of the national count for HCV and DCD; the region’s own rate for EVMP), and joins the table to the state polygons.
Each study script saves its regional table to tables/, then, for each measure, draws the ggplot2 and tmap maps and saves them to figures/<study>/.
Quarto renders the site, copying the maps for the Results page, and the publish workflow pushes it to the gh-pages branch.

Configuration
All settings are constants in R/setup.R; no environment variables or data paths are needed. The region geography comes with sRtr, and the regional counts are in the study scripts. The HRSA layer is downloaded from gisportal.hrsa.gov, so a run needs internet access to that host.
